subject: maths

moments.title: Hilbert's program and Russell's paradox
moments.body:
Hilbert proposes a program to formalise all of mathematics on a complete, consistent axiomatic basis. Every true statement should be provable; the consistency of the system should be demonstrable within itself.

Russell discovers his paradox in set theory (1901): the set of all sets that don't contain themselves. This catches Frege's Grundgesetze at the printer. Russell and Whitehead spend 10 years writing Principia Mathematica (1910-13) to construct mathematics from a careful logical foundation.
moments.takeaway: Foundations of mathematics seems shaky after Russell. Hilbert and others want to put it on firm ground.

moments.title: Gödel completeness theorem (NOT incompleteness)
moments.body:
Gödel, in his PhD thesis (age 23), proves the COMPLETENESS theorem for first-order logic: any logically valid statement in first-order logic is provable from the axioms.

This is a positive result. It suggests Hilbert's program might be achievable for richer systems.
moments.takeaway: Gödel's first major result supports Hilbert. The shocking 'incompleteness' is still a year away.

moments.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
moments.body:
Gödel publishes 'On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems'. The result devastates Hilbert's program.

Method: Gödel encodes statements about arithmetic AS arithmetic statements (Gödel numbering). The system can now 'talk about itself'. He constructs a sentence G that asserts 'G cannot be proved'.

- First incompleteness theorem: any consistent formal system expressive enough to express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
- Second incompleteness theorem: such a system cannot prove its own consistency.

Gödel is 25.

quote.text: Any effectively generated theory capable of expressing elementary arithmetic cannot be both consistent and complete.

moments.takeaway: Mathematics has fundamental gaps. There are true things it cannot prove. Hilbert's program is dead.

moments.title: Gödel emigrates
moments.body:
Gödel proves the consistency of the Continuum Hypothesis with ZFC (1940) by constructing the 'constructible universe' L. (Cohen will later prove its independence, in 1963.)

Meanwhile, he flees Nazi Europe via Siberia and arrives at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1940. He becomes a US citizen in 1948 — at the hearing, he reportedly tries to point out an inconsistency in the US Constitution, but his sponsors (Einstein and Morgenstern) cut him off.
moments.takeaway: Gödel survives WWII and settles in Princeton. He continues to do foundational work.

moments.title: Gödel's death
moments.body:
Gödel suffered chronic anxiety and paranoia. He believed his food was being poisoned and would only eat what his wife Adele prepared. When Adele was hospitalised in late 1977, Gödel stopped eating.

He died of starvation on 14 January 1978. He weighed 65 pounds.

His Princeton colleagues had tried to help. Einstein had walked daily with Gödel until his own death in 1955.
moments.takeaway: The greatest logician of the 20th century starves himself to death from paranoia.

now.title: Logic and foundations today
now.body:
We accept that mathematics has provably undecidable problems. The continuum hypothesis is independent of ZFC. Many natural questions in group theory, topology and number theory are similarly independent.

Formal verification, using proof assistants (Coq, Lean, Isabelle), is making computer-checked mathematics increasingly practical. Modern foundations include type theory, category theory, and homotopy type theory as alternatives to ZFC.
now.open_questions: Can we find 'natural' mathematical statements that are independent of ZFC? Is the consistency of ZFC actually provable (in some larger system)? What's the role of large cardinals in modern set theory? Will proof assistants ever produce mathematics that humans can't follow?

reflection: Gödel was friends with Einstein. They walked home together every day. Both made discoveries that overturned the most cherished assumptions of their fields: gravity as geometry, mathematics as incomplete. Both were exiles from Nazi-occupied Europe. What does it tell us that two of the 20th century's greatest minds ended their lives — Einstein with a relatively peaceful death, Gödel by self-imposed starvation — both having transformed their fields irreversibly?
